## Where we are

On Tuesday we ended the *Protect* step with a promise: if the data cannot leave your machine, you can **bring the model to the data** instead. Today we keep that promise with [Ollama](https://ollama.com){target="_blank"}, and use a local model in three ways:

1. **Ask it a question**, from the terminal and from R.
2. **Process data**: turn free text into columns of a `data.table`.
3. **Generate embeddings**: measure how similar two pieces of text are.

The activities are in [Lab 09](lab.qmd); keep your work in one Quarto document, `lab09.qmd`.

# Ollama in a nutshell

## What it is and why use it

Ollama runs open-weight language models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral, ...) **on your own computer**. It downloads and manages the models for you, and runs a small server in the background that the terminal, R, and other programs talk to.

Why run a model locally?

- **Privacy**: the prompt and the data never leave your machine.
- **Cost**: no per-token billing, so thousands of calls are fine.
- **Reproducibility**: you keep the exact model file; it will not change under you.

The catch: local models are **small**. They hallucinate more and follow instructions less reliably than the models you use in chat, so everything we said on Tuesday about verifying applies even more. And local is not automatically approved: it does not replace your DUA or IRB protocol. (Also, model names ending in `-cloud` run on Ollama's servers, not yours.)

## Installing Ollama and getting models

1. Download and install Ollama from <https://ollama.com/download>{target="_blank"}, and open it. On Linux, start it with `ollama serve`.
2. Pull the models we will use today:

```{.bash}
ollama pull llama3.2:1b          # Llama 3.2, 1 billion parameters (~1.3 GB)
ollama pull embeddinggemma:300m  # An embedding model (~0.6 GB)
```

3. Install the R package [`ollamar`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ollamar){target="_blank"} [^rollama]:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("ollamar")
```

A few more commands you will use:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ollama list` | Installed models and their size on disk |
| `ollama run llama3.2:1b` | Chat with a model in the terminal (`/bye` to exit) |
| `ollama ps` | Models currently loaded, and how much memory they use |
| `ollama rm <model>` | Delete a model |

The model name tells you its size: `1b` is one billion parameters. As a rule of thumb, a laptop with 8 GB of RAM runs 1--3B models comfortably and 16 GB handles ~8B.

[^rollama]: The [`rollama`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rollama){target="_blank"} package provides a more R-like interface. We use `ollamar` because it follows the official API closely and is actively maintained.

# Asking a question

## From the terminal and from R

The quickest way to try a model is the terminal:

```{.bash}
ollama run llama3.2:1b "What is INSNA Sunbelt?"
```

From R, check that Ollama is running and call `generate()`:

```{r}
#| label: ollamar-generate
#| eval: false
library(ollamar)

test_connection() # Is Ollama running?
list_models()     # Same as `ollama list`

ans <- generate(
  model  = "llama3.2:1b",
  prompt = "What is INSNA Sunbelt?"
)
resp_process(ans, "text")
```

Run it a few times. A 1B model will tell you, with great confidence, several different things about the Sunbelt conference, and some of them will be wrong. (It is the annual meeting of the International Network for Social Network Analysis.) Small models are bad at facts; they are much better at transforming text you give them.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 1: install and ask

Lab 09, Tasks 1 and 2. Install Ollama, pull the models, and ask `llama3.2:1b` questions from the terminal and from R. Note which answers are correct and which are invented.
:::

## Getting the same answer twice

An LLM samples its answer, so the same prompt usually gives different answers. Extra arguments to `generate()` are passed to the model as options, which lets us control that:

```{r}
#| label: ollamar-options
#| eval: false
ask <- function(prompt, ...) {
  generate(
    model  = "llama3.2:1b",
    prompt = prompt,
    system = "You are a concise biostatistician. Answer in one sentence.",
    output = "text",
    ...
  )
}

ask("What is a p-value?") # Different every time
ask("What is a p-value?", temperature = 0, seed = 1231) # Same every time
```

- `system`: instructions that frame every answer.
- `temperature`: 0 always picks the most likely word; higher values are more random.
- `seed`: fixes the random number generator, like `set.seed()`.

For research, record the model, prompt, system prompt, options, and seed in your Quarto document, just as you record package versions.

# Processing data

## The LLM as a function

For research we usually want **data**, not prose: a label or a yes/no that goes into a column. Ollama can force the answer to follow a JSON schema, so it always parses.

Let's code each workshop in the Sunbelt 2026 agenda by the software it teaches and its level:

```{r}
#| label: agenda
#| warning: false
library(data.table)
agenda <- fread("sunbelt2026_workshops.csv")
dim(agenda)
agenda[1:3, .(title, presenters)]
```

The schema is an R list that mirrors JSON Schema; `enum` restricts the allowed values:

```{r}
#| label: schema
#| eval: false
schema <- list(
  type       = "object",
  properties = list(
    software = list(type = "string", enum = c("R", "Python", "both", "none")),
    level    = list(
      type = "string",
      enum = c("introductory", "intermediate", "advanced")
    )
  ),
  required   = list("software", "level")
)

code_workshop <- function(description) {
  ans <- generate(
    model       = "llama3.2:1b",
    prompt      = paste(
      "Classify this workshop description. Which software does it teach,",
      "and what level is it?\n\n",
      description
    ),
    format      = schema,
    output      = "text",
    temperature = 0,
    seed        = 1231
  )
  jsonlite::fromJSON(ans)
}

codes <- lapply(agenda$description, code_workshop)
agenda[, software := vapply(codes, `[[`, "", "software")]
agenda[, level := vapply(codes, `[[`, "", "level")]
agenda[, .N, by = software]
```

Text in, a row of data out. This is the same idea as coding open-ended survey responses, one of the most useful things a local model can do with data you cannot upload.

## A valid JSON is not a correct answer

The schema guarantees the *format*, not the *content*. A 1B model will happily say an introductory R workshop is advanced Python, and the JSON will parse perfectly. Treat the model as a measurement instrument and validate it:

1. Hand-code a few descriptions yourself *before* looking at the model's answers.
2. Compute the agreement between you and the model.
3. Read the disagreements: is the model wrong, or are your categories ambiguous?
4. If you publish LLM-coded data, report the model, prompt, options, and agreement.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 2: code the workshops, then verify

Lab 09, Task 3. Hand-code five workshops, run the model on all 20, and compute the agreement. Then change one thing (the prompt, the schema, or the model) and see whether agreement improves.
:::

# Embeddings

## Text as vectors

An **embedding model** does not generate text. It maps a piece of text to a vector of numbers (here, 768 of them) so that texts with similar meaning end up close together. Search engines, recommendation systems, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are built on them.

The usual measure of similarity is the **cosine similarity**, which is 1 for vectors pointing the same way and 0 for unrelated ones. For unit-length vectors it is just a dot product, so `crossprod()` computes all pairs at once. A toy example with three "texts" in three dimensions:

```{r}
#| label: cosine-toy
emb <- cbind(
  networks = c(0.9, 0.1, 0.0),
  graphs   = c(0.8, 0.3, 0.1),
  cooking  = c(0.0, 0.2, 0.9)
)
emb <- sweep(emb, 2, sqrt(colSums(emb^2)), "/") # Unit length columns
round(crossprod(emb), 2)
```

## Embedding the Sunbelt agenda

`embed()` returns one column per input, already normalized to unit length:

```{r}
#| label: embed-agenda
#| eval: false
emb <- embed("embeddinggemma:300m", agenda$description)
dim(emb) # 768 x 20

sim <- crossprod(emb) # 20 x 20 cosine similarities

# The five workshops most similar to the first one (excluding itself)
top <- order(sim[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[2:6]
agenda[c(1, top), .(title)]
```

Connect each workshop to its three most similar ones and we get a network whose clusters are groups of related topics, found without reading a single abstract:

```{r}
#| label: embed-network
#| eval: false
library(igraph)
library(netplot)

n <- ncol(sim)
diag(sim) <- -Inf # Exclude self-loops
edges <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
  cbind(i, order(sim[i, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:3])
}))

net <- simplify(graph_from_edgelist(edges, directed = FALSE))
V(net)$name <- agenda$title

nplot(
  net,
  vertex.label   = NA,
  vertex.size    = 0.05,
  edge.width     = 0.5,
  edge.color     = ~ ego(alpha = 0.5),
  edge.curvature = 0.15
)
```

As always, look before you trust: do the clusters make sense to someone who knows the field?

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}

# Wrap-up

## Local or cloud?

| Use a local model when | Use a cloud model when |
|---|---|
| The data cannot leave the machine | The data are public or approved for that service |
| The task is narrow and repetitive: classify, extract, embed | The task needs reasoning, long context, or good code |
| You need the exact same model in two years | You need the best available quality today |

Often the answer is both: use a cloud agent to *write and test* the code against fake data (Tuesday's no-upload workflow), then run that code with a *local* model on the real data.

**Do** record the model, prompt, options, and seed; use structured output when the answer goes into a data set; and validate against your own coding. **Don't** ask a small model for facts, or assume that a parsed JSON is a correct answer.

Finish `lab09.qmd` at home if you did not get through everything; it is due Sunday as usual. Next week: the midterm hackathon.
